title: Design a Distributed Job Scheduler
oneLiner: Run millions of one-off and recurring jobs on time across a fleet of workers, as a 45-minute design round: leases, retries, at-least-once and no double runs that matter.
keyTakeaway: A job scheduler is a durable store of due times, a way to find what is due without scanning everything, and a work queue whose workers hold leases. Delivery is at least once, so jobs must be idempotent or carry a fencing token; recurring jobs are stored as their next run time, not expanded forever; and the interesting failures are a worker that stalls mid-job and a scheduler that fires the same job twice.
explanation:
Same format as the other walk-throughs: write your answer for each stage first, then compare it with the model answer and tick what you covered.

This problem looks like cron with more machines, and that is the trap. The hard parts are not parsing schedules but correctness under failure: a worker that takes a job and then crashes, freezes in a long garbage collection pause or loses its network; a scheduler node that fires a batch of jobs and dies before recording it; and a midnight peak when half the world's daily jobs are due in the same second. A strong answer separates the parts that decide when a job is due from the parts that run it, uses leases with heartbeats rather than locks held forever, and is honest that delivery is at least once.

Interviewers usually push on four things: how you find due jobs without scanning a huge table (time-bucketed indexes or partitions), what happens when a worker dies or stalls (lease expiry, retries with backoff, fencing tokens), how you stop one tenant's million jobs from starving everyone else (per-tenant queues and quotas), and how recurring schedules and time zones work. It builds on the Message Queues, Distributed Async Systems and Timeouts, Retries and Circuit Breakers lessons, and it is closely related to designing a notification system or a web crawler's frontier.
